24       This case arises out of a lawsuit filed by Plaintiff Indect USA Corp. (“Indect”) 
25  seeking a declaratory judgment that neither Indect nor the users of its products infringed 
26  on claims of U.S. Patent Number 9,594,956 (the “956 Patent”) owned by Defendant Park 
27  Assist, LLC (“Park Assist”).  Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”), ECF No. 58, ¶ 6.  
28  The matter comes before the Court on Park Assist’s Motion to Preclude Expert 
1  Testimony of Matthew A. Turk (the “Motion”) as well as the parties’ accompanying 
2  motions to file matters under seal.  ECF Nos. 138, 139, 155.              
3       Based on the parties’ briefs, evidence submitted, and applicable law, the Court 
4  denies Park Assist’s Motion to preclude Dr. Turk’s expert testimony.  The Court grants 
5  the parties’ motions to file documents associated with the subject Motion under seal. 
6  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
7       In his expert report, Dr. Turk determined Park Assist’s ‘956 Patent is invalid due to 
8  obviousness.  ECF No. 140, Ex. B (hereinafter “Turk Report”), ¶ 87.  Park Assist seeks to 
9  preclude Dr. Turk’s testimony on the grounds that Dr. Turk “fails to provide any legally 
10  adequate opinion regarding how or why the prior art references would be combined.”  
11  ECF 138, at 6.                                                            
12  II.  LEGAL STANDARDS                                                      
13       A. Expert Witnesses                                                  
14       Federal Rule of Evidence 702 establishes several requirements for admissibility of 
15  expert opinion evidence: (1) the witness must be sufficiently qualified as an expert by 
16  knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education; (2) the scientific, technical, or other 
17  specialized knowledge must assist the trier of fact either “to understand the evidence” or 
18  “to determine a fact in issue”; (3) the testimony must be “based on sufficient facts and 
19  data”; (4) the testimony must be “the product of reliable principles and methods”; and (5) 
20  the expert must reliably apply the principles and methods to the facts of the case.  Fed. R. 
21  Evid. 702.                                                                
22       Under Daubert and its progeny, the trial court is tasked with assuring that expert 
23  testimony “both rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task at hand.”  
24  Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 597 (1993).  “Expert opinion 
25  testimony is relevant if the knowledge underlying it has a valid connection to the 
26  pertinent inquiry.  And it is reliable if the knowledge underlying it has a reliable basis in 
27  the knowledge and experience of the relevant discipline.”  Primiano v. Cook, 598 F.3d 
28  558, 565 (9th Cir. 2010) (citation and quotation marks omitted).  Shaky but admissible 
1  evidence is to be attacked by cross-examination, contrary evidence, and careful 
2  instruction on the burden of proof, not exclusion.  Daubert, 509 U.S. at 596.  The judge is 
3  “to screen the jury from unreliable nonsense opinions, but not exclude opinions merely 
4  because they are impeachable.”  Alaska Rent-A-Car, Inc. v. Avis Budget Grp., Inc., 738 
5  F.3d 960, 969 (9th Cir. 2013).  In its role as gatekeeper, the trial court “is not tasked with 
6  deciding whether the expert is right or wrong, just whether his [or her] testimony has 
7  substance such that it would be helpful to a jury.”                       
8       The tests for admissibility in general, and reliability, are flexible.  Primiano, 598 
9  F.3d at 564.  The Supreme Court has provided several factors to determine reliability: (1) 
10  whether a theory or technique is testable; (2) whether it has been published in peer 
11  reviewed literature; (3) the error rate of the theory or technique; and (4) whether it has 
12  been generally accepted in the relevant scientific community.  Mukjtar v. Cal. State 
13  Univ., 299 F.3d 1053, 1064 (9th Cir. 2002) (summarizing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 592-94), 
14  overruled on other grounds by Estate of Barabin v. Asten Johnson, Inc., 740 F.3d 457, 
15  460 (9th Cir. 2014).  These factors are meant to be “helpful, not definitive.”  Kumho Tire 
16  Co. v. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137, 151 (1999).  The court “has discretion to decide how to 
17  test an expert's reliability as well as whether the testimony is reliable, based on the 
18  particular circumstances of the particular case.”  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 564 (citations and 
19  quotation marks omitted).                                                 
20       “[T]he test under Daubert is not the correctness of [experts’] conclusions but the 
21  soundness of [their] methodology.”  Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 43 
22  F.3d 1311, 1318 (9th Cir. 1995).  Once the threshold established by Rule 702 is met, the 
23  expert may testify, and the fact finder decides how much weight to give that testimony.  
24  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 565.                                                
25       After admissibility is established to the court’s satisfaction, attacks aimed at the 
26  weight of the evidence are the province of the fact finder, not the judge.  Pyramid Techs., 
27  Inc. v. Hartford Cas. Ins. Co., 752 F.3d 807, 814 (9th Cir. 2014).  The court should not 
28  make credibility determinations that are reserved for the jury.  Id.      
1       B. Patent Invalidity by Obviousness                                  
2       Under the U.S. Patent Act, an invention cannot be patented if “the subject matter as 
3  a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having 
4  ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains.”  35 U.S.C. § 103(a).  A 
5  party seeking to invalidate a patent based on obviousness must demonstrate “by clear and 
6  convincing evidence that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine the 
7  teachings of the prior art references to achieve the claimed invention, and that the skilled 
8  artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.”  Pfizer, Inc. v. 
9  Apotex, Inc., 480 F.3d 1348, 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2007).  The obviousness determination turns 
10  on underlying factual inquiries involving: (1) the scope and content of prior art, (2) 
11  differences between claims and prior art, (3) the level of ordinary skill in pertinent art, 
12  and (4) secondary considerations such as commercial success and satisfaction of a long-
13  felt need.  Procter & Gamble Co. v. Teva Pharm. USA, Inc., 566 F.3d 989, 994 (Fed. Cir. 
14  2009).                                                                    
15  III.  DISCUSSION                                                          
16       A. Testimony of Dr. Matthew Turk                                     
17       Park Assist seeks preclusion of Dr. Turk’s testimony for several reasons: (1) there 
18  is no evidence of motivation to combine, (2) the analysis fails to show how references 
19  could be combined, and (3) the analysis improperly combines multiple references.  This 
20  Court disagrees with Park Assist and finds preclusion improper.           
21            i.   Evidence of Motivation to Combine                          
22       Park Assist asserts the statements in Dr. Turk’s report are formulaic and amount to 
23  nothing more than conclusory analysis.  ECF No. 138, 2.  Park Assist further avers Dr. 
24  Turk’s testimony is completely generic due to the same standard approach he took in 
25  evaluating the combinations in his report.  Id. at 4.  Park Assist argues generic approaches 
26  like this have consistently been rejected by the Federal Circuit because “recognizing a 
27  need or problem to be solved is very different from a motivation to combine references.”  
28  Id.                                                                       
1       In support of its argument, Park Assist cites ActiveVideo Networks, Inc. v. Verizon 
2  Commc’ns, Inc. (694 F.3d 1312 (Fed. Cir. 2012)).  In ActiveVideo, the District Court 
3  found the expert’s testimony on obviousness to be conclusory when he testified, “[t]hese 
4  are all components that are modular, and when I add one, it doesn’t change the way the 
5  other works.”  Id. at 1327.  The Federal Circuit found this testimony “failed to explain 
6  how specific references could be combined, which combination(s) of elements in specific 
7  references would yield a predictable result, or how any specific combination would 
8  operate or read on the asserted claims.”  Id.  The present case differs in two critical ways, 
9  though.  First, ActiveVideo was decided on a Judgement as a Matter of Law (JMOL) 
10  motion.  While this testimony failed to persuade ultimately, Verizon’s expert was still 
11  allowed to testify.  Second, Dr. Turk’s analysis goes far beyond the generic “desire for 
12  improvement” the District Court found unpersuasive in ActiveVideo.  Dr. Turk’s report 
13  identifies specific elements and combines multiple references in great detail while 
14  analyzing five separate claims for obviousness.  Turk Report, ¶¶ 88-188.  Dr. Turk’s 
15  analysis is not conclusory, and this Court finds cross-examination the appropriate avenue 
16  for Park Assist to challenge Dr. Turk’s methodology and conclusions.      
17       Park Assist further alleges that Dr. Turk’s analysis cannot point to a motivation for 
18  improvement, which is a requirement for showing obviousness.  ECF 138, at 3.  Again, 
19  Park Assist cites ActiveVideo.  There, Verizon’s expert testified, “[t]he motivation to 
20  combine would be because you want to build something better . . . by combining these 
21  two things you could do something new that [you] hadn’t been able to do before.”  
22  ActiveVideo at 1328.  Dr. Turk’s report, by comparison, goes into significantly greater 
23  detail in its analysis and explains with specificity the improvement sought for each 
24  referenced item.  See, Turk Report ¶¶ 88-188.  Moreover, there is no requirement for 
25  explicit motivation to be stated to combine prior art references.  See, KSR Intern. Co. v. 
26  Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 419-22 (2007).                               
27       Also, as stated above, the court heard the expert’s testimony in ActiveVideo, but 
28  certain claims were adjudicated via JMOL, suggesting it was appropriate for the fact 
1  finder to hear the expert testimony even if it ultimately proved unpersuasive.   
2       “The motivation to combine prior art references can come from the knowledge of 
3  those skilled in the art, from the prior art reference itself, or from the nature of the 
4  problem to be solved.”  Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc., 949 F.3d 
5  1366, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2020).  On its face, Dr. Turk’s report meets these criteria.  His 
6  report contains analysis Park Assist can test or contest about the motivation a person of 
7  ordinary skill in the art would have to combine prior art references.  Park Assist can 
8  challenge Dr. Turk using cross-examination or its own evidence, as other courts have 
9  found when addressing factual issues on motivating prior artwork.  See, e.g., Cellular 
10  Communs. Equip., LLC v. Apple Inc., No. 6:14-cv-251, 2016 WL 6884076, at *3 (E.D. 
11  Tex. Aug. 30, 2016); Equistar Chemicals, LP v. Westlake Chem. Corp., 6:14CV68, 2016 
12  WL 4410050, at *3 (E.D. Tex. Feb. 26, 2016).                              
13            ii.  Evidence Showing How References Can Be Combined            
14       Beyond analysis requiring evidence of motivation to combine, obviousness also 
15  requires some teaching of how the references could be combined to work together.  See, 
16  Power-One, Inc. v. Artesyn Techs., Inc., 599 F.3d 1343, 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2010).  Here, 
17  Park Assist asserts Dr. Turk simply cherry picks elements from various references, gives 
18  no second thought about technical problems or challenges that may arise, and is not clear 
19  as to how his proposed combinations would work.  ECF No. 138, at 9-10.  This Court 
20  disagrees.                                                                
21       Dr. Turk’s report provides detailed analysis that could assist a jury in determining 
22  the question of invalidity of the ‘956 Patent for obviousness.  As this Court stated in 
23  Section III(a)(i), supra, Dr. Turk’s report references primary and secondary sources in 
24  analyzing the obviousness issues and demonstrates how a person of ordinary skill in the 
25  art could use the references to combine them and improve existing ideas.  Moreover, the 
26  combined references are all in the field of camera-based parking management systems.  
27  From their pleadings, it appears Park Assist’s disagreements are with the conclusions 
28  drawn by Dr. Turk and his methodology in reaching said conclusions.  This goes towards 
1  the weight, not the admissibility, of Dr. Turk’s testimony and, as previously stated, can 
2  be addressed during cross-examination or with other evidence.             
3            iii.  Alleged Improper Combination of References                
4       One of the selections of artwork Dr. Turk analyzed in his obviousness analysis is 
5  the “M3 Product.”  Regarding the M3 Product, the parties disagree on how the product 
6  has evolved and whether Dr. Turk should have addressed the evolution.  Park Assist 
7  claims, “Dr. Turk treats multiple different references related to the M3 Product as a single 
8  article – drawing his analysis from whichever reference he believes best shows a given 
9  claim element . . . Dr. Turk is thus using his single “M3” reference [as] a mishmash of 
10  different references, without any word of why this is proper and without discussing any 
11  motivation to combine these multiple M3 references.”  ECF No. 138, at 14.  Indect 
12  argues,                                                                   
13       “Park Assist cannot claim that all of the documents that constitute the M3, as 
14       set forth in Dr. Turk’s report are about a different product – they all disclose 
15       feature of the M3 sold by Park Assist before the priority date of the ‘956 
16       patent.  As such, there is nothing to combine, the documents are neither 
17       describing different products offered by Park Assist, nor describing products 
18       from Park Assist and another source.”                                
19  ECF No. 164, at 20.  The parties’ pleadings yet again indicate a reasonable disagreement 
20  on Dr. Turk’s methodology and the conclusions he reaches which are subjects 
21  appropriate for cross examination.  Park Assist fails to persuade this Court that exclusion 
22  is necessary under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 or Daubert.               
23       Park Assist claims Indect is attempting to persuade this Court to forego its 
24  responsibilities under Daubert and “leave it to Park Assist to address the baseless Turk 
25  opinion with cross examination.”  ECF No. 138, at 8.  In support of this claim, Park 
26  Assist cites Innogenetics, N.V. v. Abbott Laboratories, 512 F.3d 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2008) 
27  and Deckers Outdoor Corp. v. Romeo & Juliette, Inc., 2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 217136, 
28  *9-10 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 6, 2017).  In Innogenetics, the Federal Circuit found the district 
1  court did not abuse its discretion in precluding expert testimony on obviousness when the 
2  expert “merely list[ed] a number of prior art references and then conclude[d] with the 
3  stock phrase ‘to one skilled in the art it would have been obvious to perform’ . . . .” 
4  Innogenetics at. 1373.  The court stated, “nowhere does [the expert] state how or why a 
5  person ordinarily skilled in the art would have found the claims of the [] patent obvious in 
6  light of some combination of those particular references.”  Id. at 1373.  In Deckers, the 
7  expert proffered that it would have been obvious to modify the reference, but did not state 
8  why or provide any motivation.  Deckers at 9-10.                          
9       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court finds it offers far more than the 
10  conclusory statements described in Innogenetics and Deckers.  Dr. Turk’s report 
11  describes with specificity how the prior art references can be combined and identifies the 
12  limitations taught by each primary reference and secondary reference.  This goes well 
13  beyond conclusory statements and provides the factfinder evidence which may support 
14  Indect’s claims of obviousness.                                           
15            iv.  Scope of Testimony                                         
16       “The ultimate test of patent invalidity is one of law . . . but resolution of the 
17  obviousness issue necessarily entails several basic factual inquiries.”  Sakraida v. Ag Pro, 
18  Inc., 425 U.S. 273, 280 (1976).  To the extent that an expert purports to offer a legal 
19  opinion on an ultimate issue, such testimony must be excluded because “offering legal 
20  conclusion testimony invades the province of the trial judge.”  Nationwide v. Kass Info. 
21  Sys., Inc., 523 F.3d 1051, 1059 (9th Cir. 2008); Mukhtar, 299 F.3d at 1066 n.10 ("[A]n 
22  expert witness cannot give an opinion as to her legal conclusion, i.e., an opinion on an 
23  ultimate issue of law.").  While expert testimony can be used to provide evidence of the 
24  state of the art, how one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the prior art 
25  references, and whether one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to 
26  combine or modify prior art references in a manner that yields the claimed invention, it is 
27  improper to provide testimony that is merely a legal conclusion.          
28       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court concludes it passes muster under the 
1  reliability and relevance requirements of Daubert and Rule 702.  Therefore, Park Assist’s 
2  request to preclude Dr. Turk’s testimony entirely is denied.  Dr. Turk’s testimony, 
3  however, must not serve as a substitute for jury instructions on obviousness or make 
4  conclusory statements that the ‘956 patent should be invalidated on obviousness grounds. 
5       B. Motions to Seal                                                   
6       Concurrent with the parties’ briefing on the Turk Motion to Preclude, the parties 
7  move to file under seal portions of their briefs, declarations, and supporting exhibits.  The 
8  selections contain, reference, or discuss commercially sensitive and proprietary business 
9  data.  The documents have been previously designated “Confidential,” “Confidential – 
10  For Counsel Only,” or “Confidential – For Counsel Only – Prosecution Bar” pursuant to 
11  the Protective Order issued in this case.  See ECF No. 43.  Specifically, these selections 
12  ostensibly contain business information including trade secrets, confidential research, and 
13  other financial or commercial information.                                
14       “[C]ompelling reasons sufficient to outweigh the public’s interest in disclosure and 
15  justify sealing court records exist when such court files might . . . become a vehicle for 
16  improper purposes, such as the use of records to . . . release trade secrets.”  Kamakana v. 
17  City & Cnty. of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1179 (9th Cir. 2006).  A “trade secret may 
18  consist of any formula, pattern, device or compilation of information which is used in 
19  one’s business, and which gives him an opportunity to obtain an advantage over 
20  competitors who do not know or use it.”  The Court can seal proprietary information to 
21  protect a business from potential harm.  See Obesity Research Institute, LLC v. Fiber 
22  Research International, LLC, No. 15-CV-00595-BAS-MDD, 2017 WL 6270268, at *2 
23  (S.D. Cal. Dec. 8, 2017) (granting motion to file documents containing proprietary 
24  business information under seal).                                         
25       Accordingly, the motions to seal are granted.  Redacted versions of the 
26  aforementioned documents have been filed on the public docket.  The Clerk is directed to 
27  file unredacted versions of the documents and exhibits lodged at Docket Numbers 140 
28  and 163 under seal.                                                       
1   |}IV.   CONCLUSION 
2         Park Assist’s Motion to Preclude Expert Testimony of Dr. Matthew Turk is 
3  || DENIED.  The parties’ motions to file their pleadings related to the subject Daubert 
4   ||motion are GRANTED. 
5         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
6         Dated: September 24, 2021 
7                                                     O     ROGER T. BENIT 
                                                      United States District Judge

16       A. Testimony of Dr. Matthew Turk                                     
17       Park Assist seeks preclusion of Dr. Turk’s testimony for several reasons: (1) there 
18  is no evidence of motivation to combine, (2) the analysis fails to show how references 
19  could be combined, and (3) the analysis improperly combines multiple references.  This 
20  Court disagrees with Park Assist and finds preclusion improper.           
21            i.   Evidence of Motivation to Combine                          
22       Park Assist asserts the statements in Dr. Turk’s report are formulaic and amount to 
23  nothing more than conclusory analysis.  ECF No. 138, 2.  Park Assist further avers Dr. 
24  Turk’s testimony is completely generic due to the same standard approach he took in 
25  evaluating the combinations in his report.  Id. at 4.  Park Assist argues generic approaches 
26  like this have consistently been rejected by the Federal Circuit because “recognizing a 
27  need or problem to be solved is very different from a motivation to combine references.”  
28  Id.                                                                       
1       In support of its argument, Park Assist cites ActiveVideo Networks, Inc. v. Verizon 
2  Commc’ns, Inc. (
694 F.3d 1312
 (Fed. Cir. 2012)).  In ActiveVideo, the District Court 
3  found the expert’s testimony on obviousness to be conclusory when he testified, “[t]hese 
4  are all components that are modular, and when I add one, it doesn’t change the way the 
5  other works.”
Id. at 1327
.  The Federal Circuit found this testimony “failed to explain 
6  how specific references could be combined, which combination(s) of elements in specific 
7  references would yield a predictable result, or how any specific combination would 
8  operate or read on the asserted claims.”
Id.
  The present case differs in two critical ways, 
9  though.  First, ActiveVideo was decided on a Judgement as a Matter of Law (JMOL) 
10  motion.  While this testimony failed to persuade ultimately, Verizon’s expert was still 
11  allowed to testify.  Second, Dr. Turk’s analysis goes far beyond the generic “desire for 
12  improvement” the District Court found unpersuasive in ActiveVideo.  Dr. Turk’s report 
13  identifies specific elements and combines multiple references in great detail while 
14  analyzing five separate claims for obviousness.  Turk Report, ¶¶ 88-188.  Dr. Turk’s 
15  analysis is not conclusory, and this Court finds cross-examination the appropriate avenue 
16  for Park Assist to challenge Dr. Turk’s methodology and conclusions.      
17       Park Assist further alleges that Dr. Turk’s analysis cannot point to a motivation for 
18  improvement, which is a requirement for showing obviousness.  ECF 138, at 3.  Again, 
19  Park Assist cites ActiveVideo.  There, Verizon’s expert testified, “[t]he motivation to 
20  combine would be because you want to build something better . . . by combining these 
21  two things you could do something new that [you] hadn’t been able to do before.”  
22  ActiveVideo at 1328.  Dr. Turk’s report, by comparison, goes into significantly greater 
23  detail in its analysis and explains with specificity the improvement sought for each 
24  referenced item.  See, Turk Report ¶¶ 88-188.  Moreover, there is no requirement for 
25  explicit motivation to be stated to combine prior art references.  See, KSR Intern. Co. v. 
26  Teleflex Inc.,
550 U.S. 398, 419-22
 (2007).                               
27       Also, as stated above, the court heard the expert’s testimony in ActiveVideo, but 
28  certain claims were adjudicated via JMOL, suggesting it was appropriate for the fact 
1  finder to hear the expert testimony even if it ultimately proved unpersuasive.   
2       “The motivation to combine prior art references can come from the knowledge of 
3  those skilled in the art, from the prior art reference itself, or from the nature of the 
4  problem to be solved.”  Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc.,
949 F.3d 5
  1366, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2020).  On its face, Dr. Turk’s report meets these criteria.  His 
6  report contains analysis Park Assist can test or contest about the motivation a person of 
7  ordinary skill in the art would have to combine prior art references.  Park Assist can 
8  challenge Dr. Turk using cross-examination or its own evidence, as other courts have 
9  found when addressing factual issues on motivating prior artwork.  See, e.g., Cellular 
10  Communs. Equip., LLC v. Apple Inc., No. 6:14-cv-251,
2016 WL 6884076
, at *3 (E.D. 
11  Tex. Aug. 30, 2016); Equistar Chemicals, LP v. Westlake Chem. Corp., 6:14CV68, 2016
12 WL 4410050
, at *3 (E.D. Tex. Feb. 26, 2016).                              
13            ii.  Evidence Showing How References Can Be Combined            
14       Beyond analysis requiring evidence of motivation to combine, obviousness also 
15  requires some teaching of how the references could be combined to work together.  See, 
16  Power-One, Inc. v. Artesyn Techs., Inc.,
599 F.3d 1343, 1351
 (Fed. Cir. 2010).  Here, 
17  Park Assist asserts Dr. Turk simply cherry picks elements from various references, gives 
18  no second thought about technical problems or challenges that may arise, and is not clear 
19  as to how his proposed combinations would work.  ECF No. 138, at 9-10.  This Court 
20  disagrees.                                                                
21       Dr. Turk’s report provides detailed analysis that could assist a jury in determining 
22  the question of invalidity of the ‘956 Patent for obviousness.  As this Court stated in 
23  Section III(a)(i), supra, Dr. Turk’s report references primary and secondary sources in 
24  analyzing the obviousness issues and demonstrates how a person of ordinary skill in the 
25  art could use the references to combine them and improve existing ideas.  Moreover, the 
26  combined references are all in the field of camera-based parking management systems.  
27  From their pleadings, it appears Park Assist’s disagreements are with the conclusions 
28  drawn by Dr. Turk and his methodology in reaching said conclusions.  This goes towards 
1  the weight, not the admissibility, of Dr. Turk’s testimony and, as previously stated, can 
2  be addressed during cross-examination or with other evidence.             
3            iii.  Alleged Improper Combination of References                
4       One of the selections of artwork Dr. Turk analyzed in his obviousness analysis is 
5  the “M3 Product.”  Regarding the M3 Product, the parties disagree on how the product 
6  has evolved and whether Dr. Turk should have addressed the evolution.  Park Assist 
7  claims, “Dr. Turk treats multiple different references related to the M3 Product as a single 
8  article – drawing his analysis from whichever reference he believes best shows a given 
9  claim element . . . Dr. Turk is thus using his single “M3” reference [as] a mishmash of 
10  different references, without any word of why this is proper and without discussing any 
11  motivation to combine these multiple M3 references.”  ECF No. 138, at 14.  Indect 
12  argues,                                                                   
13       “Park Assist cannot claim that all of the documents that constitute the M3, as 
14       set forth in Dr. Turk’s report are about a different product – they all disclose 
15       feature of the M3 sold by Park Assist before the priority date of the ‘956 
16       patent.  As such, there is nothing to combine, the documents are neither 
17       describing different products offered by Park Assist, nor describing products 
18       from Park Assist and another source.”                                
19  ECF No. 164, at 20.  The parties’ pleadings yet again indicate a reasonable disagreement 
20  on Dr. Turk’s methodology and the conclusions he reaches which are subjects 
21  appropriate for cross examination.  Park Assist fails to persuade this Court that exclusion 
22  is necessary under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 or Daubert.               
23       Park Assist claims Indect is attempting to persuade this Court to forego its 
24  responsibilities under Daubert and “leave it to Park Assist to address the baseless Turk 
25  opinion with cross examination.”  ECF No. 138, at 8.  In support of this claim, Park 
26  Assist cites Innogenetics, N.V. v. Abbott Laboratories,
512 F.3d 1363
 (Fed. Cir. 2008) 
27  and Deckers Outdoor Corp. v. Romeo & Juliette, Inc.,
2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 217136
, 
28  *9-10 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 6, 2017).  In Innogenetics, the Federal Circuit found the district 
1  court did not abuse its discretion in precluding expert testimony on obviousness when the 
2  expert “merely list[ed] a number of prior art references and then conclude[d] with the 
3  stock phrase ‘to one skilled in the art it would have been obvious to perform’ . . . .” 
4  Innogenetics at. 1373.  The court stated, “nowhere does [the expert] state how or why a 
5  person ordinarily skilled in the art would have found the claims of the [] patent obvious in 
6  light of some combination of those particular references.”
Id. at 1373
.  In Deckers, the 
7  expert proffered that it would have been obvious to modify the reference, but did not state 
8  why or provide any motivation.  Deckers at 9-10.                          
9       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court finds it offers far more than the 
10  conclusory statements described in Innogenetics and Deckers.  Dr. Turk’s report 
11  describes with specificity how the prior art references can be combined and identifies the 
12  limitations taught by each primary reference and secondary reference.  This goes well 
13  beyond conclusory statements and provides the factfinder evidence which may support 
14  Indect’s claims of obviousness.                                           
15            iv.  Scope of Testimony                                         
16       “The ultimate test of patent invalidity is one of law . . . but resolution of the 
17  obviousness issue necessarily entails several basic factual inquiries.”  Sakraida v. Ag Pro, 
18  Inc.,
425 U.S. 273, 280
 (1976).  To the extent that an expert purports to offer a legal 
19  opinion on an ultimate issue, such testimony must be excluded because “offering legal 
20  conclusion testimony invades the province of the trial judge.”  Nationwide v. Kass Info. 
21  Sys., Inc.,
523 F.3d 1051, 1059
 (9th Cir. 2008); Mukhtar, 299 F.3d at 1066 n.10 ("[A]n 
22  expert witness cannot give an opinion as to her legal conclusion, i.e., an opinion on an 
23  ultimate issue of law.").  While expert testimony can be used to provide evidence of the 
24  state of the art, how one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the prior art 
25  references, and whether one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to 
26  combine or modify prior art references in a manner that yields the claimed invention, it is 
27  improper to provide testimony that is merely a legal conclusion.          
28       Having reviewed the Turk Report, this Court concludes it passes muster under the 
1  reliability and relevance requirements of Daubert and Rule 702.  Therefore, Park Assist’s 
2  request to preclude Dr. Turk’s testimony entirely is denied.  Dr. Turk’s testimony, 
3  however, must not serve as a substitute for jury instructions on obviousness or make 
4  conclusory statements that the ‘956 patent should be invalidated on obviousness grounds. 
5       B. Motions to Seal                                                   
6       Concurrent with the parties’ briefing on the Turk Motion to Preclude, the parties 
7  move to file under seal portions of their briefs, declarations, and supporting exhibits.  The 
8  selections contain, reference, or discuss commercially sensitive and proprietary business 
9  data.  The documents have been previously designated “Confidential,” “Confidential – 
10  For Counsel Only,” or “Confidential – For Counsel Only – Prosecution Bar” pursuant to 
11  the Protective Order issued in this case.  See ECF No. 43.  Specifically, these selections 
12  ostensibly contain business information including trade secrets, confidential research, and 
13  other financial or commercial information.                                
14       “[C]ompelling reasons sufficient to outweigh the public’s interest in disclosure and 
15  justify sealing court records exist when such court files might . . . become a vehicle for 
16  improper purposes, such as the use of records to . . . release trade secrets.”  Kamakana v. 
17  City & Cnty. of Honolulu,
447 F.3d 1172
, 1179 (9th Cir. 2006).  A “trade secret may 
18  consist of any formula, pattern, device or compilation of information which is used in 
19  one’s business, and which gives him an opportunity to obtain an advantage over 
20  competitors who do not know or use it.”  The Court can seal proprietary information to 
21  protect a business from potential harm.  See Obesity Research Institute, LLC v. Fiber 
22  Research International, LLC, No. 15-CV-00595-BAS-MDD,
2017 WL 6270268
, at *2 
23  (S.D. Cal. Dec. 8, 2017) (granting motion to file documents containing proprietary 
24  business information under seal).                                         
25       Accordingly, the motions to seal are granted.  Redacted versions of the 
26  aforementioned documents have been filed on the public docket.  The Clerk is directed to 
27  file unredacted versions of the documents and exhibits lodged at Docket Numbers 140 
28  and 163 under seal.
